chapters.title: The Bhote Koshi–Trishuli disaster
chapters.body:
At **08:37:10** a slab of rock and glacier ice broke from the north face of **Langtang Lirung**. In the next six hours the debris flow it became ran **200 km** down the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani, past the Nepal–China border, a dry port, a trekking town, a cascade of hydropower plants and a string of river towns.

It was Nepal's deadliest disaster since the 2015 earthquake. As of 22 September the NDRRMA counts **1,451 bodies or remains recovered and 5,705 people missing**; China reported 43 dead and 519 missing. The government puts damage and losses at **US$2.70 bn**. All figures are still provisional.

This story follows the front minute by minute, then goes town by town with the sharpest before-and-after imagery that is openly available. Every layer is open data; the sources are listed in each chapter.

chapters.title: A corridor of trade, power and towns
chapters.body:
The Bhote Koshi valley carries Nepal's main road to China. The **Rasuwagadhi–Kerung crossing** had only just reopened: the July 2025 glacial-lake flood from Tibet had closed it for **177 days**, and it reopened on 2026-01-01 on a 91 m Bailey bridge. It had been open 237 days when this flood came, 414 days after the last one.

The river is also one of Nepal's densest hydropower corridors. The government counts **13 projects totalling 759 MW** hit by this flood — 7 operating (250 MW) and 6 under construction (509 MW) — with thousands of workers in tunnels and camps.

About **70,030 people** live within 500 m of the path and **209,751** within 2 km (Kontur, ~0.7 km² cells, so an order of magnitude). OpenStreetMap held **6,966 buildings** within 200 m of the channel on 25 August.

chapters.title: The mountain fails
chapters.body:
Seismometers caught it. USGS catalogued a **magnitude 5.2 “landslide” signal** (us7000tbwb) at 08:37:10 — a hand-placed origin; EMSC and later phase picks put it at **08:37:44** — and GFZ an Mw 5.7 event with a landslide signature, while Nepal's Department of Mines and Geology first logged an M4.4 earthquake. Chinese seismologists found smaller signals at 06:04, 06:50 and 08:15–08:19: the slope was already moving, and radar had shown up to 30 cm of creep in the weeks before.

UNOSAT mapped the **detachment zone — 1.96 km²** — on Landsat 9 that same day; the scar drops about 1,100–1,200 m. Seismic estimates of the volume range from about 10 million to 500 million m³; no before-and-after elevation model has measured it yet. There was **no significant rain** (8.8 mm in the previous three days), so rainfall-based warnings never triggered. A **second failure** followed at 11:45:35 (M4.2); USGS has since relocated it to beside the lower barrier lake.

The swipe compares Sentinel-2 in November 2025 with 16 September: the grey scar of the flow runs from the mountain down to the valley floor. Switch the right side to the Legion-6 scene of 2026-09-18 for a sub-metre view; no sub-metre image of the source exists from before the event.

chapters.title: Twenty kilometres in seven minutes
chapters.body:
In the upper gorge the front moved at **25–49 m/s (90–180 km/h)**. It crossed into Tibet and back and reached **Rasuwagadhi about seven minutes** after the detachment; CCTV at Gyirong Port caught it at 08:44. The Rasuwagadhi gauge sent its last reading, 1.62 m, at 08:40 — far below its 6 m warning level — and then fell silent. **Timure** was hit about a minute later, **Syabrubesi** at 08:50–09:00.

The camera follows the modelled front (arrival times from the gauges, eased between reports) and the timeline slows down while the front is fastest. Settlements flash as it reaches them.

chapters.title: A lake behind the debris
chapters.body:
Where the Chhochen Khola meets the Purepu–Chusumdo valley, just inside Tibet, the debris dammed the river. UNOSAT mapped the lake from Cartosat-3 on 28 August at **11.9 ha**; China's Ministry of Water Resources put it at about **2–2.5 million m³**. It **overflowed on 28 August at about 15:35**, pausing rescue work downstream for three hours and raising the river about 0.6 m, and drained on 29–30 August. A second lake of 19.5 ha formed just below the source; it was assessed as low risk.

Swipe between two PlanetScope frames: hours after the flow on 2026-08-26 and two days later on 2026-08-28, with the lake ponded behind the fan.

chapters.title: Rasuwagadhi, destroyed twice
chapters.body:
The border crossing had been rebuilt after the 2025 glacial-lake flood. The left side is NEA Engineering's **3.5 cm drone survey** of 2025-09-01 — the road, the river and the Miteri Bridge at the crossing (left) down to Timure (right) — laid over PlanetScope from May 2026. The right side is WorldView-3 on 2026-08-27, the day after: the road, the bridges and the valley floor are scoured to bare gravel.

Use the labels to switch scenes: WorldView-2 in 2021, before either flood; Legion-4, Pelican and HOT's mosaic after. The front reached the crossing about seven minutes after the detachment, **31 minutes before** the SMS alert went out.

chapters.title: Timure dry port
chapters.body:
Timure's customs yard handled the trade that crossed at Rasuwagadhi. It had the least warning of any town. Fifteen customs staff lost contact; **more than 300 queued vehicles, around 1,000 electric vehicles and over 400 containers** were swept away. Copernicus EMS graded **372 buildings destroyed** here.

The default swipe is WorldView-2 in 2021 against Legion-4 on 2026-09-08. Switch the left side to PlanetScope in May 2026 to see the port as it was, already rebuilt after the 2025 flood.

chapters.title: Syabrubesi
chapters.body:
Syabrubesi sits where the Bhote Koshi meets the Langtang Khola, at the start of the Langtang trail. GeoEye-1 in 2023 shows the town climbing terraced slopes above a narrow river; WorldView-3 on 2026-08-27 shows the confluence and the riverside town under a single sheet of grey sediment. EMS graded **323 buildings destroyed**.

Chilime's powerhouse at Syabrubesi was buried; rescuers reached it through 250 m of tunnel and found five NEA staff dead. Among the alternates is a PlanetScope frame taken at **11:29 that same morning**, about two and a half hours after the front passed, and HOT's mosaic of the Vantor scenes from 27 August to 8 September.

chapters.title: The gauges went silent
chapters.body:
DHM's river gauges report every ten minutes. The three upstream stations — Rasuwagadhi, Syabrubesi and Betrawati — **stopped transmitting while still below their warning levels**: they were destroyed before they could register the flood. A gauge-based alarm could not have fired for the upper valley.

Downstream the record survives. Galchhi rose **about 8.8 m in half an hour**; Devghat peaked at **6.57 m and 5,850 m³/s at 16:00**, below its warning level — a 2–3-year flood by the time it reached the plains.

chapters.title: Faster than the warning
chapters.body:
DHM's forecasters learned of the wave around 09:00. At **09:15 the alert was confirmed and at 09:16 a mass SMS** went out: 679,295 messages to phones in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan — **38.8 minutes** after the detachment.

By then the front had passed Rasuwagadhi, Timure and Syabrubesi. Betrawati got about ten minutes. At Tribhuvan Trishuli school about 900 pupils were evacuated roughly ten minutes before the water arrived. Downstream the lead time grew: about an hour at Galchhi, more than three hours at Mugling.

Negative bars mean the flood arrived before the SMS. The warning latency was longer than the flood's travel time to the first three towns — the central finding of Acharya & Paudel's analysis.

chapters.title: Down the Trishuli
chapters.body: Below Syabrubesi the valley narrows past **Tiru** (where more than 500 people were still unaccounted for weeks later) and the Upper Trishuli hydropower sites, then opens at **Betrawati** and **Trishuli Bazar**. The front slowed to a few metres per second but carried the valley floor with it.

chapters.title: 804 workers still missing
chapters.body:
The government counts **13 hydropower projects (759 MW)** and 5 solar plants hit. On 23 September the Energy Minister told Parliament that 11 plants were shut, **410 MW was off the grid** — more than a tenth of Nepal's capacity — and **804 workers were still missing**.

The toll concentrated at the construction sites. At **Upper Trishuli-1** (216 MW, 84% built, US$647 M) 1,433 people were on site; 439 are missing and more than 90% of the upper dam is gone. Thirty-one bodies were recovered from the rebar mesh of its Audit-3 tunnel at Hakubesi. At **Upper Trishuli-3B** the workers' quarters were buried: 178 missing. At Upper Trishuli-3A two workers were rescued alive from a tunnel on day ten.

chapters.title: Simle and the Upper Trishuli-3B camp
chapters.body:
Just above Betrawati, the Upper Trishuli-3B project had its powerhouse and workers' camp on the valley floor at Simle. The quarters were buried; an excavation 2 m below the new riverbed found only an office foundation. **178 workers** are missing here.

The left side is NEA Engineering's **6 cm drone survey** of September 2025, a year before the flood, laid over WorldView-2 from May 2024; upstream is on the left. No clear sub-metre image exists after the flood: cloud or haze covers every scene of this reach. The right side is Sentinel-2 (10 m) on 2026-09-21; switch it to PlanetScope taken at **10:46 on 26 August**, about an hour and a half after the front passed — hazy, but the new riverbed is plain.

chapters.title: Betrawati
chapters.body:
At Betrawati the Phalakhu Khola joins the Trishuli, and both gauges here went silent at 09:20. WorldView-2 in May 2024 shows the town and bridges; Legion-6 on 2026-09-07 (partly cloudy) and PlanetScope on 28 August show the debris fan that filled the valley. Betrawati had about **ten minutes** of warning.

UNOSAT saw the Uttargaya Dham temples and Shree Ram Mandir destroyed; the government's assessment adds Betrawati's historic treaty stone (Sandhishila) to 47 damaged heritage assets.

chapters.title: Trishuli Bazar and Bidur
chapters.body:
In February 2026 (Legion-6, 0.35 m) the Trishuli ran between Trishuli Bazar and Bidur about as wide as a road. On 2026-09-08 (WorldView-2) it is a braided gravel bed several hundred metres wide, the **Trishuli bridge is gone**, and riverside streets are erased. Tribhuvan Trishuli school evacuated about 900 pupils roughly ten minutes before the water arrived.

Copernicus EMS graded **2,479 buildings destroyed** in the Bidur area — the largest count of any mapped town; the government counts 3,026 buildings affected in Bidur municipality. Sugatpur Buddhist Vihara was destroyed.

chapters.title: Six hours to the plains
chapters.body: Below Galchhi the Trishuli runs beside the Prithvi Highway, Nepal's busiest road. The Phurke gauge at Malekhu crossed its danger level at 11:43 and was swept away with the bridge beside it. The flood passed Mugling by 13:00 and reached the Narayani at Devghat in mid-afternoon, peaking there at 16:00. The camera pulls back as the valley widens.

chapters.title: Devghat and the Narayani
chapters.body: At Devghat the flood entered the Narayani. The peak — 6.57 m, 5,850 m³/s — stayed below the warning level: a 2–3-year flood here. Bodies were carried far further: most were recovered in Chitwan and Nawalparasi, and some reached Uttar Pradesh in India. Sentinel-2: 2025-11-05 against 2026-09-21.

chapters.title: Seen from the ground
chapters.body:
Open, geotagged photos and video of this disaster are scarce. Everything found under an open licence is on the map — click a point to open it:

- **205 photos from before** (Wikimedia Commons and Flickr), including a series taken along the Trishuli on 24 August, two days before the flood
- **246 street-level frames** from KartaView on the Galchhi–Devghat highway
- **CCTV clips from Gyirong Port**, released into the public domain, showing the flood arriving at 08:44
- **Umbra radar images** of the source and the barrier lake (CC BY 4.0), which see through monsoon cloud
- a few **news videos** on YouTube (links only, placed approximately at the towns they show)

No openly licensed, geotagged ground video from after the flood could be found; Mapillary's archive needs a sign-in to search.

chapters.title: Counting the buildings
chapters.body:
The government's Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment counts **7,570 buildings affected** in 15 municipalities — 3,026 in Bidur alone — home to about 8,317 households and 32,963 people.

Satellite mapping agrees on the pattern. Copernicus EMS graded four towns within days: **3,571 buildings destroyed**, 427 damaged and 687 possibly damaged. UNOSAT flagged 5,048 potentially affected buildings along the whole corridor and 10 heritage sites damaged or destroyed, among them Rasuwa Fort at the border; the government lists 47 heritage assets and 18 schools damaged and 4 health posts destroyed.

Of 6,966 buildings mapped in OpenStreetMap within 200 m of the channel the day before, **3,056** now lie in stripped or buried ground or have vanished from the map.

chapters.title: 39 of 58 bridges gone
chapters.body:
Bridges tell the story best, because a bridge cannot drift downstream the way bodies do. HOT's survey of 58 named bridges found **39 washed out** — 23 of 27 in Rasuwa, 11 of 20 in Nuwakot, 5 of 8 in Dhading and none in Gorkha. The government counts **33 road bridges washed out** and 4 damaged — 3 km of bridge — plus 68 trail-bridge spans and **69 km of road**, including the whole 55 km from Betrawati to Rasuwagadhi.

Army Bailey bridges went in at Phalakhu (70 m), Betrawati (72 m) and Syabrubesi (76 m). Downstream the river cut 70 m of the Prithvi Highway at **Krishnabhir**, closing Nepal's busiest road — about 14,000 vehicles a day — from 30 August to 17 September.

chapters.title: What the satellites saw
chapters.body:
Comparing Sentinel-2 before (October–November 2025) and after (September 2026) along all 200 km, change detection finds **15.95 km²** of vegetation or river channel replaced by bare debris within 500 m of the path — **83%** of it above Bidur, where the flow was fastest. HOT mapped 31.7 km² of flood extent from imagery on 27 August.

Monsoon cloud hid parts of every scene; masked areas are not counted, so these are lower bounds.

chapters.title: 30.5 million cubic metres
chapters.body:
A government model puts **30.5 million m³** of debris on the valley floor over the 94 km from Timure to Malekhu — 53% of it on the long reach from Haku to Devighat. Clearing only the settlements would mean moving about 1.8 million m³.

UNOSAT mapped **65 km² of mudflow and rockflow** from the source to below Devghat on images from 26–27 August. How much rock and ice fell in the first place is still open: seismic estimates range from about 10 to 500 million m³.

chapters.title: 1,451 dead, 5,705 missing
chapters.body:
The count grew for weeks as recovery reached the upper valley. By 22 September the NDRRMA counted **1,451 dead — 585 men, 336 women and 530 partial remains — and 5,705 missing**; 13,795 people had been rescued. The police keep a separate register: 1,452 dead and 4,718 missing on 23 September. Duplicate reports have been removed from the missing lists since 21 September, so the two will converge.

The missing include hydropower workers, drivers queued at the border, trekkers and residents, and **more than 600 foreigners from 35 countries**. DNA samples had been taken from 1,286 bodies and 1,997 relatives by 21 September. China reported 43 dead and 519 missing.

chapters.title: Carried 250 km
chapters.body:
Where bodies were recovered is not where people died. By 21 September **821 of 1,451** had been found in Chitwan and the two Nawalparasi districts, on the Narayani plains 150–250 km from the source — 57% of the total. Some reached Uttar Pradesh in India.

Rasuwa's count rose last, from 13 on 30 August to 236, as searchers dug into the upper valley; 31 of those bodies came out of the Upper Trishuli-1 tunnel at Hakubesi on 20–21 September. (One chart in SitRep #20 swaps Rasuwa and Nuwakot; the figures here follow its district table and the police count.)

chapters.title: US$2.70 bn of damage and losses
chapters.body:
The government's assessment puts damage and losses at **NPR 408 billion (US$2.70 bn)** and the cost of recovery at **US$4.77 bn**, most of it long-term. Energy is the largest item — US$997 M of damage and losses and US$2.58 bn to rebuild — ahead of lost livelihoods and trade (US$965 M) and homes (US$422 M).

The figures were cut off on 3 September, before most of the upper valley had been reached. On 24 September Nepal's foreign minister told the UN General Assembly that losses exceed US$5 billion.

chapters.title: Faster than any warning built on rain or rivers
chapters.body:
**The trigger was dry.** No rain fell at the source, so rainfall thresholds never fired.

**The river gauges died first.** The three upstream stations went silent below their warning levels; the instrument that could have raised the alarm was destroyed by the thing it measured.

**Seismometers saw it at once.** The 08:37 signal was recorded worldwide within minutes but logged in Nepal as an earthquake. A seismic trigger for mass-flow alerts on this corridor could have bought the first towns minutes they did not have.

**It happened twice in 14 months.** The 2025 flood came from Tibet, this one from Nepal's own side; both hit the same crossing, dry port and hydropower cascade. Recovery built back in the same place.

ICIMOD — Kyirong–Rasuwa flood 2026

chapters.title: Methods, data and caveats
chapters.body:
**Flow front.** Acharya & Paudel's centreline from the scar to Devghat, timed by DHM gauge arrivals and reports. The front moves at constant speed between reports and eases between speeds around each one; it shows when the front passed, not a hydraulic simulation.

**Imagery.** Town close-ups stream full-resolution scenes straight from the Vantor Open Data Program and Planet's Crisis Response release (both CC BY-NC 4.0), NEA Engineering's drone orthophotos on OpenAerialMap (CC BY 4.0) and HOT's post-event mosaic, chosen per town for the least cloud after checking every available scene. Nothing is re-hosted. Sentinel-2 fills in where no sub-metre scene exists.

**Official figures.** Tolls follow NDRRMA's situation reports (the police register is noted where it differs); damage, costs and the debris model come from the government's Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (cut-off 3 Sep); missing hydropower workers from the Energy Minister's statement to Parliament. Satellite damage maps are Copernicus EMS's and UNOSAT's.

**Change detection.** Sentinel-2 pixels where NDVI fell at least 0.2 to below 0.25 while the surface brightened, or water became bright bare ground, within 500 m of the path; cloud, shadow and snow masked in both scenes. A screening map.

**Buildings** are OpenStreetMap footprints as of 25 August; "hit" means inside a change area, or deleted after the event with nothing redrawn there. **Damage grades** are Copernicus EMS's; **bridges** are HOT's field survey. **Media** are only items with an open licence and a location; YouTube videos are links. **All figures are provisional.**
